 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1810628#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Seemingly random, difficult to predict bit stream created by a deterministic algorithm

A **pseudorandom binary sequence** (**PRBS**), **pseudorandom binary code** or **pseudorandom bitstream** is a [binary sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_sequence) that, while generated with a deterministic [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm), is difficult to predict[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-TTI-1) and exhibits statistical behavior similar to a truly random sequence. PRBS generators are used in [telecommunication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunication), such as in analog-to-information conversion,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-2) but also in [encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encryption), [simulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulation), [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation) technique and time-of-flight [spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscopy). The most common example is the [maximum length sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_length_sequence) generated by a (maximal) [linear feedback shift register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear-feedback_shift_register) (LFSR). Other examples are [Gold sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_code) (used in [CDMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDMA) and [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System)), [Kasami sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasami_code) and [JPL sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JPL_sequence), all based on LFSRs.

In [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunication), pseudorandom binary sequences are known as **pseudorandom noise codes** (**PN** or **PRN codes**) due to their application as [pseudorandom noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_noise).

## Details

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=1)]

A binary sequence (BS) is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence)      a  0   , … ,  a  N − 1     {\displaystyle a_{0},\ldots ,a_{N-1}}   of     N   {\displaystyle N}   bits, i.e.

      a  j   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle a_{j}\in \{0,1\}}   for     j = 0 , 1 , . . . , N − 1   {\displaystyle j=0,1,...,N-1}  .

A BS consists of     m = ∑  a  j     {\displaystyle m=\sum a_{j}}   ones and     N − m   {\displaystyle N-m}   zeros.

A BS is a **[pseudorandom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandomness) binary sequence** (PRBS) if[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-3) its [autocorrelation function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocorrelation_function), given by

     C ( v ) =  ∑  j = 0   N − 1    a  j    a  j + v     {\displaystyle C(v)=\sum _{j=0}^{N-1}a_{j}a_{j+v}}

has only two values:

     C ( v ) =   {    m ,    if    v ≡ 0   (   mod   N )        m c ,    otherwise            {\displaystyle C(v)={\begin{cases}m,{\mbox{ if }}v\equiv 0\;\;({\mbox{mod}}N)\\\\mc,{\mbox{ otherwise }}\end{cases}}}

where

     c =    m − 1   N − 1      {\displaystyle c={\frac {m-1}{N-1}}}

is called the *duty cycle* of the PRBS, similar to the [duty cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty_cycle) of a continuous time signal. For a [maximum length sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_length_sequence), where     N =  2  k   − 1   {\displaystyle N=2^{k}-1}  , the duty cycle is 1/2.

A PRBS is 'pseudorandom', because, although it is in fact deterministic, it seems to be random in a sense that the value of an      a  j     {\displaystyle a_{j}}   element is independent of the values of any of the other elements, similar to real random sequences.

A PRBS can be stretched to infinity by repeating it after     N   {\displaystyle N}   elements, but it will then be cyclical and thus non-random. In contrast, truly random sequence sources, such as sequences generated by [radioactive decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay) or by [white noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_noise), are infinite (no pre-determined end or cycle-period). However, as a result of this predictability, PRBS signals can be used as reproducible patterns (for example, signals used in testing telecommunications signal paths).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4)

## Practical implementation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=2)]

Pseudorandom binary sequences can be generated using [linear-feedback shift registers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear-feedback_shift_register).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-5)

Some common[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-Bloopist-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-10) sequence generating [monic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monic_polynomial) are

 PRBS7 =      x  7   +  x  6   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{7}+x^{6}+1}   PRBS9 =      x  9   +  x  5   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{9}+x^{5}+1}   PRBS11 =      x  11   +  x  9   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{11}+x^{9}+1}   PRBS13 =      x  13   +  x  12   +  x  2   + x + 1   {\displaystyle x^{13}+x^{12}+x^{2}+x+1}   PRBS15 =      x  15   +  x  14   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{15}+x^{14}+1}   PRBS20 =      x  20   +  x  3   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{20}+x^{3}+1}   PRBS23 =      x  23   +  x  18   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{23}+x^{18}+1}   PRBS31 =      x  31   +  x  28   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{31}+x^{28}+1}

An example of generating a "PRBS-7" sequence can be expressed in C as

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    uint8_t start = 0x02;
    uint8_t a = start;
    int i;
    for (i = 1;; i++) {
        int newbit = (((a >> 6) ^ (a >> 5)) & 1);
        a = ((a << 1) | newbit) & 0x7f;
        printf("%x\n", a);
        if (a == start) {
            printf("repetition period is %d\n", i);
            break;
        }
    }
}
```

In this particular case, "PRBS-7" has a repetition period of 127 values.

## Notation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=3)]

The PRBS*k* or PRBS-*k* notation (such as "PRBS7" or "PRBS-7") gives an indication of the size of the sequence.     N =  2  k   − 1   {\displaystyle N=2^{k}-1}   is the maximum number[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §3  of bits that are in the sequence. The *k* indicates the size of a unique [word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_(computer_architecture)) of data in the sequence. If you segment the *N* bits of data into every possible word of length *k*, you will be able to list every possible combination of 0s and 1s for a k-bit binary word, with the exception of the all-0s word.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §2  For example, PRBS3 = "1011100" could be generated from      x  3   +  x  2   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}+x^{2}+1}  .[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-Bloopist-6) If you take every sequential group of three bit words in the PRBS3 sequence (wrapping around to the beginning for the last few three-bit words), you will find the following 7 word arrangements:

```
"1011100" → 101
  "1011100" → 011
  "1011100" → 111
  "1011100" → 110
  "1011100" → 100
  "1011100" → 001 (requires wrap)
  "1011100" → 010 (requires wrap)
```

Those 7 words are all of the      2  k   − 1 =  2  3   − 1 = 7   {\displaystyle 2^{k}-1=2^{3}-1=7}   possible non-zero 3-bit binary words, not in numeric order. The same holds true for any PRBS*k*, not just PRBS3.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §2

Pseudorandom binary sequence

# Pseudorandom binary sequence

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1810628#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Seemingly random, difficult to predict bit stream created by a deterministic algorithm

A **pseudorandom binary sequence** (**PRBS**), **pseudorandom binary code** or **pseudorandom bitstream** is a [binary sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_sequence) that, while generated with a deterministic [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm), is difficult to predict[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-TTI-1) and exhibits statistical behavior similar to a truly random sequence. PRBS generators are used in [telecommunication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunication), such as in analog-to-information conversion,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-2) but also in [encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encryption), [simulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulation), [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation) technique and time-of-flight [spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscopy). The most common example is the [maximum length sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_length_sequence) generated by a (maximal) [linear feedback shift register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear-feedback_shift_register) (LFSR). Other examples are [Gold sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_code) (used in [CDMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDMA) and [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System)), [Kasami sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasami_code) and [JPL sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JPL_sequence), all based on LFSRs.

In [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunication), pseudorandom binary sequences are known as **pseudorandom noise codes** (**PN** or **PRN codes**) due to their application as [pseudorandom noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_noise).

Details

# Details

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=1)]

A binary sequence (BS) is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence)      a  0   , … ,  a  N − 1     {\displaystyle a_{0},\ldots ,a_{N-1}}   of     N   {\displaystyle N}   bits, i.e.

      a  j   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle a_{j}\in \{0,1\}}   for     j = 0 , 1 , . . . , N − 1   {\displaystyle j=0,1,...,N-1}  .

A BS consists of     m = ∑  a  j     {\displaystyle m=\sum a_{j}}   ones and     N − m   {\displaystyle N-m}   zeros.

A BS is a **[pseudorandom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandomness) binary sequence** (PRBS) if[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-3) its [autocorrelation function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocorrelation_function), given by

     C ( v ) =  ∑  j = 0   N − 1    a  j    a  j + v     {\displaystyle C(v)=\sum _{j=0}^{N-1}a_{j}a_{j+v}}

has only two values:

     C ( v ) =   {    m ,    if    v ≡ 0   (   mod   N )        m c ,    otherwise            {\displaystyle C(v)={\begin{cases}m,{\mbox{ if }}v\equiv 0\;\;({\mbox{mod}}N)\\\\mc,{\mbox{ otherwise }}\end{cases}}}

where

     c =    m − 1   N − 1      {\displaystyle c={\frac {m-1}{N-1}}}

is called the *duty cycle* of the PRBS, similar to the [duty cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty_cycle) of a continuous time signal. For a [maximum length sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_length_sequence), where     N =  2  k   − 1   {\displaystyle N=2^{k}-1}  , the duty cycle is 1/2.

A PRBS is 'pseudorandom', because, although it is in fact deterministic, it seems to be random in a sense that the value of an      a  j     {\displaystyle a_{j}}   element is independent of the values of any of the other elements, similar to real random sequences.

A PRBS can be stretched to infinity by repeating it after     N   {\displaystyle N}   elements, but it will then be cyclical and thus non-random. In contrast, truly random sequence sources, such as sequences generated by [radioactive decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay) or by [white noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_noise), are infinite (no pre-determined end or cycle-period). However, as a result of this predictability, PRBS signals can be used as reproducible patterns (for example, signals used in testing telecommunications signal paths).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4)

Practical implementation

# Practical implementation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=2)]

Pseudorandom binary sequences can be generated using [linear-feedback shift registers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear-feedback_shift_register).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-5)

Some common[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-Bloopist-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-10) sequence generating [monic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monic_polynomial) are

 PRBS7 =      x  7   +  x  6   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{7}+x^{6}+1}   PRBS9 =      x  9   +  x  5   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{9}+x^{5}+1}   PRBS11 =      x  11   +  x  9   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{11}+x^{9}+1}   PRBS13 =      x  13   +  x  12   +  x  2   + x + 1   {\displaystyle x^{13}+x^{12}+x^{2}+x+1}   PRBS15 =      x  15   +  x  14   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{15}+x^{14}+1}   PRBS20 =      x  20   +  x  3   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{20}+x^{3}+1}   PRBS23 =      x  23   +  x  18   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{23}+x^{18}+1}   PRBS31 =      x  31   +  x  28   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{31}+x^{28}+1}

An example of generating a "PRBS-7" sequence can be expressed in C as

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    uint8_t start = 0x02;
    uint8_t a = start;
    int i;
    for (i = 1;; i++) {
        int newbit = (((a >> 6) ^ (a >> 5)) & 1);
        a = ((a << 1) | newbit) & 0x7f;
        printf("%x\n", a);
        if (a == start) {
            printf("repetition period is %d\n", i);
            break;
        }
    }
}
```

In this particular case, "PRBS-7" has a repetition period of 127 values.

Notation

# Notation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pseudorandom_binary_sequence&action=edit&section=3)]

The PRBS*k* or PRBS-*k* notation (such as "PRBS7" or "PRBS-7") gives an indication of the size of the sequence.     N =  2  k   − 1   {\displaystyle N=2^{k}-1}   is the maximum number[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §3  of bits that are in the sequence. The *k* indicates the size of a unique [word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_(computer_architecture)) of data in the sequence. If you segment the *N* bits of data into every possible word of length *k*, you will be able to list every possible combination of 0s and 1s for a k-bit binary word, with the exception of the all-0s word.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §2  For example, PRBS3 = "1011100" could be generated from      x  3   +  x  2   + 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}+x^{2}+1}  .[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-Bloopist-6) If you take every sequential group of three bit words in the PRBS3 sequence (wrapping around to the beginning for the last few three-bit words), you will find the following 7 word arrangements:

```
"1011100" → 101
  "1011100" → 011
  "1011100" → 111
  "1011100" → 110
  "1011100" → 100
  "1011100" → 001 (requires wrap)
  "1011100" → 010 (requires wrap)
```

Those 7 words are all of the      2  k   − 1 =  2  3   − 1 = 7   {\displaystyle 2^{k}-1=2^{3}-1=7}   possible non-zero 3-bit binary words, not in numeric order. The same holds true for any PRBS*k*, not just PRBS3.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_binary_sequence#cite_note-O150-4): §2
